An Illustrated Victorian Mystery · Book 1

The Snuffbox

October 1881
The Wager Ledger
An illustrated edition · Complete original story

The commission came to Baker Street on a Saturday, in the person of Sir Hilary Venn, a bank director with a red face and a grievance he could not prove. He had been losing at whist all spring at the Reform Club, steadily and without explanation. He was too proud to take it to the committee and too sure of it to let it drop. He wanted someone to sit in the card room on Tuesday night as his guest and tell him whether he was a fool.

The young man he had been sent to was seven-and-twenty, very thin, and in arrears with his landlady. He listened with his eyes closed and his fingertips together and asked three questions, none of which Sir Hilary understood the point of. Then he named a fee that made Sir Hilary blink, and accepted the commission the way he accepted most things that autumn: impatiently, and for the rent.

On Tuesday he walked down to Pall Mall through a city tearing itself up to lay itself down again. The new telephone company had strung its wires from chimney to chimney like the rigging of some vast becalmed ship. The underground railway breathed sulphur up through the gratings. A theatre on the Strand had just been lit entirely by electricity, and the newsboys were shouting about the Transvaal in the tone they kept for news nobody wanted. He noticed all of it, as he noticed everything, and it interested him no more than the weather.

Sir Hilary introduced him to the card room as a nephew. Nobody believed it, and nobody much cared. He took a chair by the fire with a review he did not read, and he sat so still that within ten minutes the room had forgotten him, as rooms forget a draught they have got used to.

He watched Captain Desmond Ashe. Ashe was a pleasant, sunburnt man, elected that spring, who had served somewhere hot and won at cards steadily, never greedily, with the air of being as surprised by his luck as anyone. He kept a flat silver snuffbox at his right hand. The young man watched him deal three hands and watched where the box sat each time.

For that hour, the other three men at the Captain's table were merely part of the problem's furniture. One of them was the Captain's partner, a grey-haired gentleman in his late forties who played his cards without comment and looked at his watch at the end of every hand. The young man filed him with the chairs and the clock.

At twenty-six minutes past nine, the Captain dealt again. The young man got up, crossed to the table, and asked if he might look at the snuffbox.

He did it pleasantly. He held the box up to the gasolier and tilted the lid, admired the work, and remarked that he had never seen the inside of a lid polished so like a looking-glass. "You can see the ceiling rose in it," he said to the table at large. "One could read a card in it, if one were dealt across it." He took a pinch and did not sneeze. He observed, as if apologising for the liberty, that the Captain had no brown at his nostril and none on his handkerchief. In his experience, he said, a man who kept so fine a box and never used it kept it for some other purpose.

Then he put the box down beside the Captain's hand and stepped back. The thing was done.

What happened next was what he had expected, and he watched it with the mild satisfaction of a chemist whose solution has turned the predicted colour.

Captain Ashe went first red, then white. His opponents pushed their chairs back. At the next table Sir Hilary closed his eyes like a man whose tooth has finally been pulled. Two tables away a member set down his glass so carefully that everyone heard it. Somebody said "Good God" under his breath, and somebody else said "Steady." The whole room did what rooms do at a scandal: it moved, and pretended not to be moving.

Except for one man.

The grey-haired partner had not moved at all. He had not pushed back his chair or looked at the Captain. He had not even looked at the young man, whose demonstration had just shown that every rubber this gentleman had won in the Captain's company that spring was, in some degree, stolen. His face had not changed. If anything, the young man thought later, it had become more itself, as though the noise around him had given its stillness something to stand against.

Into the silence the gentleman said, "I believe it is still my lead," and led the king of hearts.

That was the moment the young man's attention caught on him, and having caught, it would not come free.

The gentleman played the hand out. There were nine tricks left, and he played every one of them correctly, against two opponents who could barely see their cards and a partner who no longer looked at his own. He neither hurried nor lingered. When the last trick was gathered, he consulted his watch, made a brief note in a small green book, and then took a fold of banknotes from his pocketbook. He did not count them. He seemed to know the sum already, to the shilling. He divided them between the two men who had lost to him and the Captain that spring and asked them to excuse him. Nobody at the table, the young man was quite sure, understood why he had done any of it.

The young man understood part of it. A hand that has been dealt is played. What the money had cost was a matter for the man's own books, not for the committee. What he could not understand was the temperature. He had seen composure before: in soldiers, in surgeons, in two or three very good criminals. This was not composure. Composure is a lid held down on something. This looked as though there was nothing under the lid at all, or as though whatever was there had been put in order so long ago that it no longer needed holding.

He did not ask the man's name. It would have looked strange, and in any case he had been engaged to watch Captain Ashe.

He left soon after, with Sir Hilary's envelope in his breast pocket. There was no cab on the rank. He turned up his collar and walked.

Somewhere along Waterloo Place he became aware that the grey-haired gentleman was walking ahead of him in the fog. He did not follow the man, exactly. Their road was the same for a while, and he simply did not overtake.

The gentleman walked at a pace that was neither fast nor slow, and over the next six hundred yards it did not vary by a hair. He did not hurry at the crossings or slow at the corners. When a hansom swung out of Regent Street close enough to spatter his trousers, he neither checked nor stepped aside. He arrived at the kerb at the moment the road was clear, as if he had seen the gap coming before the cabman had.

The young man, whose mind could never be kept idle, began counting the gentleman's steps between one gas lamp and the next. He counted again at the next lamp, and the next. The lamps were not evenly spaced, so the counts varied, but the length of the stride did not. He could have measured the street with it.

Then the gentleman turned off into one of the quiet streets behind Regent Street, and the fog closed over him. The young man walked on north to Baker Street and, by morning, had very nearly forgotten him.

Very nearly. Some weeks later, indexing the autumn's cases, he came to Sir Hilary's commission. Under it he wrote a line that had nothing to do with the Captain:

The partner. Played the hand out. Returned his winnings without counting. Did not look at me once. Stride constant to a hair. Name unknown.

He looked at it for a moment, decided it was not a question anyone was paying him to answer, and turned the page.

At twenty minutes past eight the next morning, in a quiet house in that quiet street behind Regent Street, the water for the master's shave arrived at eighty-four degrees Fahrenheit. By twenty-five minutes past, the young footman who had carried it up was no longer in the household's employ.

There was no scene. The master did not raise his voice, which no one in the house had ever heard raised. He took a slim thermometer in a tortoiseshell case from its place beside the basin, read it, put it back, and said, "You will be paid to the end of the month, Robert. Thank you." Then he lathered his face with the cooling water anyway, because it was there, and because the hour for shaving was the hour for shaving.

Below stairs, the steward took the news with a long breath through the nose. He was a Frenchman of some fifty years whose waist had thickened and whose good humour had not. He gave Robert a glass of wine, a written character more generous than strictly true, and the advice to try a house where the master owned no thermometer. "There are many," he said. "Most, in fact. It is a large city." Then he went up to the hall, where someone had left a gas jet burning in the daylight, and turned it out with the particular firmness of a man who had once paid for that mistake himself.

In the study, a small green ledger lay open on the desk where its owner had left it the night before. It held nine years of short entries, almost all of them wagers on the exact minute at which something would happen, and almost all placed with nobody but himself. The latest read:

11 Oct. That the second rubber will be concluded by a quarter to ten. Lost. Rubber abandoned, 9h 41m. Cause: Venn's guest.

The steward, dusting, did not read it. He never did. But he closed the book, as he did every morning, and squared it on the blotter so that its flyleaf faced upward. On the flyleaf, in the same square, unhurried hand as every entry inside, was written:

P. Fogg. 7, Savile Row.
